judgment.rationale: Both are Performance Objectives under the same Topic (2. Length), Sub-Theme (Primary Measures), Theme (Mensuration and Geometry), and Grade (PRIMARY TWO), same rank. The second SFI (385b944a) has pupils compare natural/non-standard units of length (e.g. arm's length), while the first SFI (1e15584c) has pupils use metres and centimetres as standard measuring units. Experiencing and comparing natural units and their variability pedagogically motivates and supports the transition to formal standard units, so proficiency in the second supports success in the first. This is a substantive developmental progression (natural-to-standard units), not mere shared hierarchy or wording; hence buildsTowards second_to_first rather than relatesTo.

Shared LC tags (perimeter, length, regular) and token overlap corroborate topical coherence rather than establishing the relation by themselves.

judgment.rationale: Both are PRIMARY ONE Performance Objectives under the same 'Addition' topic. The first objective covers adding two or three whole numbers from 1 to 8 with sum not up to 10; the second extends this to numbers from 0 to 9 with sum not greater than 18 (larger addend range and larger sums). This is a substantive increase in numeric complexity within the same addition skill, so proficiency in the smaller-range addition supports success in the broader-range addition, justifying a first-to-second developmental direction over a symmetric relatesTo. Same-rank direction is grounded in the specific range/sum extension rather than shared hierarchy or token overlap alone.

judgment.rationale: Both are Performance Objectives under the same Primary Two Topic '1. Addition' (same rank, rank_gap 0). First objective is 'add 3-digit numbers without exchanging or renaming'; second is 'add 2-digit numbers with exchanging or renaming'. The substantive pair-specific difference is the introduction of exchanging/renaming (carrying), a more complex procedure. Proficiency in adding without renaming is a foundational addition skill that supports success in adding with renaming, consistent with the source objective sequencing (without-renaming objectives precede the with-renaming objective). This supports a same-rank developmental direction from first to second rather than mere shared-topic co-occurrence. Shared LC tokens (addition, digit, renaming) reflect the same skill family and reinforce coherence but do not by themselves set direction.

judgment.rationale: Both are PRIMARY ONE Performance Objectives under Sub-Theme 'Basic Operations' (same grade rank 0), but in distinct Topics (second: '2. Subtraction'; first: '4. Subtraction'). The second objective, 'subtract from whole numbers not greater than 18,' is a core computational subtraction skill, while the first, 'cross-check the correctness of subtraction in everyday life,' is a higher-order verification skill that presupposes the ability to perform subtraction. Proficiency in actually subtracting substantively supports success in cross-checking subtraction correctness, justifying a same-rank developmental direction from second to first. Shared hierarchy and 'subtraction' token/tag overlap alone are noted but the pair-specific dependency (computation preceding verification) carries the judgment.

judgment.rationale: First objective is 'multiply numbers using repeated additions' (Primary Two, Topic Multiplication); second is 'add 2-digit numbers with exchanging or renaming' (Primary Two, Topic Addition). Both sit in the same Grade/Theme/Sub-Theme (Basic Operations), but shared hierarchy alone is not decisive. Substantively, multiplication via repeated addition depends on competent addition of multi-digit numbers, so proficiency in the addition objective (second) supports success in the repeated-addition multiplication objective (first). This is a same-rank pair (both PRIMARY TWO), but the pair-specific conceptual dependency—addition underpinning repeated-addition multiplication—provides substantive developmental evidence for second_to_first. Token/trigram overlap is largely generic stem wording ('pupils','should','numbers') and not itself the basis.

The first objective is the foundational skill 'find missing numbers in an open sentence,' while the second objective is 'solve simple related quantitative aptitude problems'—its LC clarifies these are quantitative aptitude problems 'related to/on open sentences,' i.e., applied/extension problems that draw on the same open-sentence concept. Proficiency in finding missing numbers plausibly supports success in the related applied problem-solving objective, supporting a first-to-second developmental direction rather than the reverse. Same rank, but the foundational-to-application relationship provides substantive evidence for direction beyond the shared parent/topic and generic wording overlap (able/be/pupils/should/to).
